Table 1:Prompt switching on T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute.Achievement: fraction of videos reflecting the new prompt.
T2V-CB: official benchmark score[46].
Quality and Overall follow VBench[20], with Achievement as the semantic score.

Figure 3:User study.Preference (%) for+ RGon the same prompt pair from 20 raters, judged on consistency (no unwanted change beyond the requested one), adherence to the new prompt, and overall preference.
RG is largely preferred for adherence and overall, with consistency slightly below parity.

Figure 4:Qualitative results on T2V-CompBench.The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch.
Without RG, the video keeps the initial state after the switch, whereas RG enables the new state to appear while the subject and scene layout remain consistent.
SF: Self Forcing, CF: Causal Forcing, MF: MemFlow, IR: Infinity-RoPE, LL: LongLive, AF: Anchor Forcing.
(a)StoryEval
(a)StoryEval
(b)InteractiveBench

Figure 6:Noise level and step schedule.Top: noise levelτ\tauwith our scheduleλ=(1,0.5,0,0)\lambda=(1,0.5,0,0). Bottom: residual added in full (λi=1\lambda_{i}=1) at the listed steps, withτ=850\tau=850. The frame before the switch (yellow neon sign) is shown on the top.

Figure 7:Context inertia by category.Fraction of pairs that switch to the new prompt when the switch chunk is regenerated with part of the cache hidden, on Self Forcing (left) and LongLive (right).Naivedenotes the base model. The number of pairs per category is in parentheses. Hiding the whole context recovers most switches, whereas a single cached chunk or the sink alone recovers little.

Figure 8:Step-wise prompt sensitivity under visible context.At each denoising stepiiof the switch chunk, the noisy input is fixed and the prompt sensitivitySi​(𝒞)S_{i}(\mathcal{C})is measured under each visible context𝒞\mathcal{C}on 100 pairs (log scale, shaded bands show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals). Numbers next to the step-1 points giveρ1\rho_{1}, the values of Fig.2(b). “Oldest chunk only” keeps only the oldest chunk still cached, which is chunk 1 for Self Forcing, whose rolling window has dropped chunk 0, and the sink (chunk 0) for LongLive.

Figure 9:VBench Quality penalizes the requested change.In each example, the top row is the base model and the bottom row is RG, and the dashed bar marks the prompt switch.
The examples are from LongLive (top), Causal Forcing (middle) and Infinity-RoPE (bottom).
The gray numbers give the VBench dimension scores of the base model and of RG.
RG follows the new prompt while the base model keeps the old state, yet RG scores lower on aesthetic quality, subject consistency and imaging quality, respectively.

Figure 10:Frames of the switch chunk.LongLive (top) and Anchor Forcing (bottom). In each example, the first row is the base model, which continues the previous state. The second row empties the cache at the switch, as in the no-context condition of Sec.3, and follows the new prompt but loses the scene in the switch chunk. The third row is RG, which realizes the new state within the switch chunk while preserving the subject and background.
Figure 11:Qualitative results on T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute.Each example shows a base model (top) and the same model with RG (bottom). The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch.
Figure 12:Qualitative results on StoryEval.Each example shows a base model (top) and the same model with RG (bottom) over three events. The white-to-black bars mark the two prompt switches.

Figure 13:Qualitative results on InteractiveBench.Each example shows a base model (top) and the same model with RG (bottom) over six prompts in 60 s, one frame per prompt. The white-to-black bars mark the five prompt switches.

Figure 14:On the choice of noise levelτ\tau.Achievement (left) and imaging quality relative to the base model (right) on 100 pairs. Dashed lines mark the base models. Achievement rises withτ\tauthroughout, whereas imaging quality holds up toτ=850\tau=850(circled) and drops sharply beyond, which is where the restored chunk no longer preserves the subject (Fig.6).

Figure 15:Qualitative results on T2V-CompBench action binding.The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch, at which a second subject is added to the prompt. Without RG the video keeps the initial scene, whereas with RG the new subject appears within the first chunks after the switch while the original subject and background are preserved.

Figure 16:Qualitative results on Rolling Forcing.T2V-CompBench dynamic attribute. In each example, the top row is Rolling Forcing and the bottom row is Rolling Forcing with RG. The white-to-black bar marks the prompt switch.
(a)Self Forcing
(a)Self Forcing
(b)LongLive

Figure 18:Alternatives to residual guidance.Achievement, Quality and scene change (object-masked DreamSim) across the switch for the base model, residual guidance (shaded) and alternatives that weaken the context, strengthen the prompt, change the erase strength, or use the cache-free reconstruction in other ways (prompt-difference (B−-A) residual, direct reconstruction, same-chunk correction, pure substitution, redraw initialization), on 100 dynamic attribute pairs with Self Forcing (circles) and LongLive (squares). Vertical lines mark residual guidance. Scene change was not measured for the variants without a marker in the right panel.Naivedenotes the base model.

Figure 19:Qualitative comparison of the alternatives.For each switch, the top row shows a frame before the switch and the bottom row a frame from the last chunk after it, on Self Forcing (top) and LongLive (bottom). Only RG shows the new prompt while keeping the scene. Removing the context or reconstructing the chunk directly redraws the whole scene, previous chunk only changes the scene or the wrong attribute, cross-attention scaling and same-chunk correction add artifacts, and cache logit, CFG and redraw initialization keep the old state. See Fig.18for the quantitative comparison.

Figure 20:Scene cuts on Infinity-RoPE.Each panel shows three consecutive prompts that keep the subject and replace the scene.
The top row is Infinity-RoPE and the bottom row is Infinity-RoPE with RG, generated from the same seed.
Dashed lines mark the prompt switches.
Infinity-RoPE often remains in the first scene or partially updates the scene,
whereas RG moves to each new scene at the switch while retaining the subject.

Figure 21:Failure cases.In each example, the top row is the base model and the bottom row is RG. The first frame is the last frame before the switch, and the dashed bar marks the prompt switch.Left: insufficient prompt response.The requested removal of an object (LongLive), change of illumination (SWIFT) or change of pose (MemFlow, InteractiveBench) is not realized.Right: unintended changes.The switch is realized, but a spoon and a hand appear (Anchor Forcing), the glass acquires a handle (Self Forcing), or the cup itself turns into a planet (Anchor Forcing, StoryEval).
